title: Agent Authorization vs. Authentication
summary: 401 or 403, invalid_token or insufficient_scope. The two checks an agent request passes through, the error codes that tell them apart, and why an agent needs two identities where a person needs one.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**Authentication and authorization are not two settings on one dial. They are two checks, run in a fixed order, and the wire protocol has told them apart for thirty years.**


RFC 9110 defines 401 as a request that "lacks valid authentication credentials for the target resource", and 403 as a server that "understood the request but refuses to fulfill it". RFC 6750 splits the OAuth layer the same way:` invalid_token` returns 401,` insufficient_scope` returns 403.


The common failure is not that engineers cannot recite those codes. It is that agent platforms collapse them into one log line reading "access denied", so the incident review starts from a category instead of a cause, and the wrong layer gets hardened.


This is not an argument that agents need a new access-control model. They need the existing one applied twice, because an agent carries two principals where a person carries one.


The check worth running today: grep your agent gateway for the place it turns a downstream 401 or 403 into a generic error, and stop it doing that.
